Empire State Building. The 102-story Art Deco skyscraper completed in 1931 in Manhattan, rising 1,250 feet to the roof and 1,454 feet with its antenna. It dominated as the world's tallest building for over forty years and remains an iconic symbol of American industrial ambition and 1930s modernism. Designed by the architectural firm Shreve, Lamb and Harmon, it was completed in just 410 days, an engineering feat for the Depression era. The tower rises 102 stories with 6,514 windows, featuring an Art Deco aesthetic with limestone and granite cladding and aluminum and stainless steel accents. It held the title of world's tallest building from 1931 until 1972, when the Willis Tower, formerly the Sears Tower, was completed in Chicago. The building contains approximately 2.7 million square feet of office and commercial space across its thirty-seven million cubic feet of volume. It anchors the Manhattan skyline from multiple vantage points and serves as a major tourist destination with an observation deck on the eighty-sixth floor. Built during the Great Depression, it symbolizes American economic resilience and capitalist optimism during economic crisis.
